With Negative Appraisals absent and no threat/appraisal content linking to preventability, this strategy feels weakly grounded relative to the formulation and selected items.

vignette: Six months ago, Rafael Vargas lost control of his sedan during a sudden downpour when a semi-truck hydroplaned across the median and slammed directly into his lane. The impact crumpled the driver’s side door, and for hours in the emergency bay, the coarse, abrasive weave of the torn seatbelt strap pressed against his shoulder, leaving a physical imprint that never quite faded. Today, those recollections do not settle into the past; they press forward with a visceral immediacy that makes ordinary moments feel as sharp as the moment of impact. The images of the crushed fenders and shattered glass surface without warning, forcing their way into his thoughts during routine chart reviews, yet the moment the scene begins to clarify, he abruptly stops, pulling the memory backward before he can fully recall the exact sequence of events. This unrelenting quality of recall has fundamentally altered how he processes his surroundings. Because the recollections arrive with such raw intensity, they instantly amplify his reactivity to everyday stimuli. Whenever he encounters the specific rough, fibrous texture of industrial rope, or hears the familiar voice of his brother on the phone, the sensory cue immediately pulls his attention toward the wrecked vehicles now parked along the arterial roads he once navigated without hesitation. The moment his eyes lock onto a dented car or a cracked windshield, the physiological alarm dictates his next move. To manage the rising panic, Rafael immediately retreats into his established routines of suppression. He stops taking pleasant activities off the table, cancels weekend plans, and deliberately steers his mind away from any reflection on the crash, convincing himself that mental distance is the only way to navigate the day. The unrelenting flood of images leaves him emotionally drained, and because he cannot stop them from surfacing, he relies entirely on his avoidance strategies to function. He consistently denies himself the chance to sit in a car, avoids any situation that puts his body under physical stress, and forces himself to avoid thinking about the event whenever the pictures intrude. These consistent efforts to suppress or physically withdraw, however, only train his nervous system to scan for danger, which makes the next trigger arrive more swiftly. When a colleague accidentally bumps his shoulder in the scrub room, the familiar pressure instantly reignites the alarm, proving that his attempts to control the response only keep the triggers active. He had come to believe that keeping his body perfectly still and his mind deliberately blank was the only way to survive another surprise. The hospital has become a landscape of careful navigation rather than a place of practice. On his morning rounds, Rafael deliberately avoids the lower parking garage where a previous collision had left a row of crushed sedans, taking a long detour past the administrative offices that leaves him perpetually rushed and emotionally exhausted before he even reaches the wards. The distance he maintains extends to his marriage. His wife, Elena, watches him meticulously avoid any shared activity that might provoke a physical or emotional response. She pleads with him to resume their weekly Sunday drives along the coast, but the mere thought of the open road triggers the same uncontrolled surge of crash imagery that once left him breathless. He is certain that engaging with the past will only cost him his stability, so he has withdrawn completely from family dinners and hospital social events. He sought counseling not because he forgot the accident, but because the silence in their home had grown too heavy to bear, and he is desperately hoping for a way to walk back into his own life without waiting for the next impact.
